{{Short description|Mathematical function in measure theory}}
{{More footnotes|date=May 2022}}

{{lowercase title}}
In [[measure theory]], a branch of mathematics that studies generalized notions of volumes, an '''s-finite measure''' is a special type of [[measure (mathematics)|measure]]. An s-finite measure is more general than a finite measure, but allows one to generalize certain proofs for finite measures.

The s-finite measures should not be confused with the [[σ-finite measure|σ-finite (sigma-finite) measures]].

== Definition ==
Let <math> (X, \mathcal A ) </math> be a [[measurable space]] and <math> \mu </math> a measure on this measurable space. The measure <math> \mu </math> is called an s-finite measure, if it can be written as a [[countably many|countable]] sum of [[finite measure]]s <math> \nu_n </math> (<math> n \in \N </math>),<ref name="Kallenberg21" />
{{bi|1=<math> \mu= \sum_{n=1}^\infty \nu_n. </math>}}

== Example ==
The [[Lebesgue measure]] <math> \lambda </math> is an s-finite measure. For this, set
{{bi|1=<math> B_n= (-n,-n+1] \cup [n-1,n) </math>}}
and define the measures <math> \nu_n </math> by
{{bi|1=<math> \nu_n(A)= \lambda(A \cap B_n) </math>}}
for all measurable sets <math> A </math>. These measures are finite, since <math> \nu_n(A) \leq \nu_n(B_n)=2 </math> for all measurable sets <math> A </math>, and by construction satisfy
{{bi|1=<math> \lambda = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \nu_n. </math>}}
Therefore the Lebesgue measure is s-finite.

== Properties ==

=== Relation to σ-finite measures ===
Every [[sigma-finite measure|σ-finite measure]] is s-finite, but not every s-finite measure is also σ-finite.

To show that every σ-finite measure is s-finite, let <math> \mu </math> be σ-finite. Then there are measurable disjoint sets <math> B_1, B_2, \dots </math> with <math> \mu(B_n)< \infty </math> and
{{bi|1=<math> \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty B_n=X </math>}}
Then the measures
{{bi|1=<math> \nu_n(\cdot):= \mu(\cdot \cap B_n) </math>}}

are finite and their sum is <math> \mu </math>. This approach is just like in the example above.

An example for an s-finite measure that is not σ-finite can be constructed on the set <math> X=\{a\} </math> with the [[sigma-algebra|σ-algebra]] <math> \mathcal A= \{\{a\}, \emptyset\} </math>. For all <math> n \in \N </math>, let <math> \nu_n </math> be the [[counting measure]] on this measurable space and define
{{bi|1=<math> \mu:= \sum_{n=1}^\infty \nu_n. </math>}}
The measure <math> \mu </math> is by construction s-finite (since the counting measure is finite on a set with one element). But <math> \mu </math> is not σ-finite, since
{{bi|1=<math> \mu(\{a\})= \sum_{n=1}^\infty \nu_n(\{a\})= \sum_{n=1}^\infty 1= \infty. </math>}}
So <math> \mu </math> cannot be σ-finite.

=== Equivalence to probability measures ===
For every s-finite measure <math> \mu =\sum_{n=1}^\infty \nu_n</math>, there exists an [[equivalent measure|equivalent]] [[probability measure]] <math> P </math>, meaning that <math> \mu \sim P </math>.<ref name="Kallenberg21" /> One possible equivalent probability measure is given by
{{bi|1=<math> P= \sum_{n=1}^\infty 2^{-n} \frac{\nu_n}{\nu_n(X)}. </math>}}
